question: Does elevated blood p-tau217 predict incident MCI in cognitively unimpaired older adults? Both studies follow cognitively unimpaired adults (population class: cognitively unimpaired older adults) with the same channel (blood Alzheimer biomarkers). P-1403 uses PREVENT-AD, a research cohort with a first-degree family history of AD, mean age 65. P-1421 uses SNAC-K, a random community sample aged 60+, median age 72. The following differences are allowed and recorded as candidate explanations: family-history enrichment, age distribution, matrix and assay, the exposure contrast and threshold, the MCI definition, the model and the horizon. The titles give opposite answers: 'Plasma p-tau217 identifies cognitively normal older adults who will develop cognitive impairment' against 'no biomarker was associated with MCI development from normal cognition'.
metric: Hazard ratio with hazard ratio. P-1403 uses Cox models by plasma A/T group against A-T-, adjusted for age at biomarker classification, sex and education. P-1421 uses multistate Markov models on an age time scale; its basic model is adjusted for sex and education, which matches P-1403's adjustment set.

figures.P-1403: Plasma A+T+ vs A-T-: HR 7.81 (95% CI 3.92-15.59), P < 0.001 (16/21 progressed against 25/127). A-T+ vs A-T-, a p-tau217-only contrast within amyloid-negative participants: HR 4.25 (1.60-11.31), P = 0.004 (5/7 progressed). A+T- vs A-T-, amyloid alone: HR 1.14 (0.58-2.24), null. T+ is p-tau217 > 3.98 pg/mL, 2 SD above the mean of Abeta-PET-negative CU adults; 28 of 215 are T+.
figures.P-1421: NC to MCI, serum p-tau217 high vs low (0.134 pg/mL, the Youden cut-off for 10-year all-cause dementia; 803 high of 2148): basic HR 1.07 (0.73-1.56); fully adjusted 1.19 (0.75-1.88). Abeta42/40 low vs high: 0.98 (0.72-1.34). Continuous splines and combinations of p-tau217, NfL and GFAP were also null for NC to MCI.
figures.comparison: A+T+: 3.92-15.59 against 0.73-1.56 (basic) or 0.75-1.88 (fully adjusted); the intervals do not overlap under either model. A-T+: 1.60-11.31 against 0.73-1.56 (basic, the matched adjustment set); they do not overlap, by a margin of 0.04. Against the fully adjusted 0.75-1.88 they overlap. This is a significant estimate against a non-significant one with non-overlapping intervals, which the rule counts. Amyloid alone is null in both papers (1.14 against 0.98), so the amyloid arm adds no disagreement.

matched_figure_check: No reconciling figure is printed. P-1421 has no A/T classification and no AD-anchored p-tau217 threshold. Its under-78 subgroup and its analysis excluding baseline MCI for NC to MCI are only in Supplementary Tables S2/S3 and S6/S7. P-1403 prints no whole-sample single-marker or continuous p-tau217 hazard ratio: its continuous analysis is ROC AUC, and its threshold sensitivity is in Supplementary Tables S7-S12. The one shared contrast, amyloid alone, agrees, but it is a different factor and does not reconcile the p-tau217 arm.
performance_validity: Not a performance comparison (association hazard ratios). P-1403's AUCs (0.66-0.82) are far below 0.97.

candidate_explanations.difference: Population: family-history-enriched research volunteers (mean age 65 at classification) against a random community sample aged 60+ (865 of 2148 aged 78 or over).
candidate_explanations.quote: a longitudinal observational study of individuals with a first-degree family history of AD

candidate_explanations.difference: Exposure contrast and threshold: joint A/T groups compared with the double-negative reference, with T+ set 2 SD above Abeta-PET-negative CU adults (13% of the sample, specificity 97% for progression), against a single-marker high/low split at a dementia-optimised cut-off (37% 'high').
candidate_explanations.quote: Cut-offs: 0.057 for Aß−42/40 ratio, 1.512 pg/mL for p-tau181, 0.134 pg/mL for p-tau217

candidate_explanations.difference: Threshold performance in P-1403: its AD-anchored tau cut-off is highly specific but insensitive for all-cause MCI, so the T+ group is a small, extreme group.
candidate_explanations.quote: gave good to excellent specificity (97% for plasma, 95% for CSF, and 100% for PET), but low sensitivity (34%, 45%, and 17%, respectively) at identifying CU who will develop MCI.

candidate_explanations.difference: MCI definition: blinded consensus requiring 1.0 SD impairment plus a subjective complaint and/or observed decline, against a psychometric 1.5 SD criterion in one domain with reversion modelled.
candidate_explanations.quote: participants needed to have a subjective memory complaint21 and/or have an objective decline witnessed over multiple cognitive follow-ups.

candidate_explanations.difference: Model and competing transitions: multistate Markov model on an age time scale with death as an absorbing state, where direct NC-to-dementia transitions are forced through MCI, against a Cox model on time since plasma.
candidate_explanations.quote: The direct transition from normal cognition to dementia was not allowed; individuals who progressed directly from normal cognition to dementia were assumed to have passed through a MCI phase, although this was not observed due to intermittent observation.

candidate_explanations.difference: Matrix and assay: plasma on an in-house Gothenburg Simoa against serum on the ALZpath Simoa kit; P-1421 states its cut-offs may not carry to other platforms.
candidate_explanations.quote: Third, our results based on cut-offs derived within the SNAC-K cohort, may not fully extend to more diverse populations or alternative laboratory platforms.

candidate_explanations.difference: Small exposure groups and horizon: 21 A+T+ and 7 A-T+ participants over a mean of 5.65 years, against 803/1345 over a mean of 9.6 years. The authors ask for caution.
candidate_explanations.quote: Given this limitation and the fact that 20% of our reference group developed MCI, the HRs between groups should be interpreted with caution.

reason: Same clinical question (blood p-tau217 and incident MCI in cognitively unimpaired older adults), same metric (HR) and a matched adjustment set. P-1403's p-tau217-positive groups carry HRs of 7.81 (3.92-15.59) and 4.25 (1.60-11.31), and both intervals exclude P-1421's 1.07 (0.73-1.56). The A+T+ contrast also excludes the fully adjusted 1.19 (0.75-1.88). No figure in either paper under the other's condition closes the gap, and on amyloid alone the two agree (both null). The pair qualifies as an unresolved discrepancy. The A-T+ margin is thin (0.04, basic model only), and the candidate explanations (enriched against community population, extreme-group AD-anchored contrast against a dementia-optimised single-marker split, MCI definition, multistate model, assay, small groups) are not shown by either paper to be sufficient.

quotes.quote: Cox proportional hazard models indicated a greater progression rate in A+T+plasma and A−T+plasma compared to A−T−plasma individuals (HR = 7.81 [95% CI = 3.92 to 15.59] and HR = 4.25 [1.60–11.31] respectively).

Cox proportional hazard models were used to assess the risk of MCI progression by AT group and linear mixed models were used to assess longitudinal cognitive changes across the biomarker groups with the addition of age at the biomarker classification, sex, and years of education as covariates.

Seventy-six percent (16/21) of the A+T+plasma group developed MCI compared to 23% (14/60) in the A+T−plasma group, 71% (5/7) in the A−T+plasma group, and 21% (25/127) in the A−T−plasma group (Figure 1A).
There were no differences between A+T−plasma and A−T−plasma group (HR = 1.14, P = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.58 to 2.24).
P-tau217 High vs Low 81/803 vs 230/1345 1.07 (0.73, 1.56) 1.19 (0.75, 1.88) (Table 2, From NC to MCI: transitions/participants, basic, fully adjusted)
Hazard Ratios (HR) with 95% Conﬁdence Intervals (CI) are derived from multistate Markov models, using age as time scale. The basic model is adjusted for sex and education
No association was found between AD blood biomarkers and the progression from normal cognition to MCI.
Elevated NfL and GFAP were linked to reduced MCI reversion to normal cognition, whereas no biomarker was associated with MCI development from normal cognition.
